pairs.rationale: Both introduce Paul as Christ Jesus' apostle through God's will and address saints. Corinthians names Timothy and its Corinth/Achaia recipients; Ephesians has no named co-sender and preserves the original brackets around in Ephesus.
Both give grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. This is a shared greeting formula addressed to different communities, not an additional event.

Both bless the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Ephesians names every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ; Peter's letter names merciful new birth and living hope through Jesus' resurrection.

Both connect divine purpose in Christ with a holy calling or life and a time before the present ages. Ephesians says chosen before the world's foundation; Timothy's letter names purpose and grace before the ages. The temporal expressions remain distinct.

Both relate adoption as sons to God's action through Jesus Christ. Galatians describes sending and redeeming through the Son and then the Spirit's cry; Ephesians emphasizes predestination according to God's good pleasure rather than repeating that sequence.

The praise-of-His-glory refrain recurs after the inheritance and prior-hope statements. Here it specifically names the glory of His grace and favor in the Beloved. This is an internal doxological pattern, not an identical additional benefit.

Both join redemption with forgiveness. Ephesians says transgressions, through His blood and according to grace's riches; the actual Colossians unit says sins and does not include an added through-His-blood clause.

Ephesians describes grace lavished in wisdom and understanding; Colossians prays for knowledge of God's will in spiritual wisdom and understanding. The related intellectual vocabulary belongs to a declaration in one and a petition in the other.

Both describe a divine mystery made known to believers. Ephesians names God's will and good pleasure; Colossians describes prior hiding, present disclosure and Christ in you as hope of glory. Their stated content and emphasis remain distinct.

Both place all things in the heavens and on earth in relation to Christ. Ephesians speaks of summing them up in Him at the fullness of times; Colossians speaks of reconciliation and peace through the cross's blood. The actions are not made identical.

Both describe an inheritance connected with divine provision. Ephesians names being allotted an inheritance according to predestining purpose; Colossians thanks the Father for enabling a share in the saints' inheritance in light. The formulations differ.

Praise of His glory repeats the earlier refrain about the glory of His grace. Here it follows we who hoped beforehand in Christ. The comparison preserves the additional prior-hope wording without assigning the we group an unprinted ethnic identity.

Both describe divine sealing and the Spirit. Corinthians also names establishing, anointing and the Spirit's pledge in hearts; Ephesians names hearing the gospel, believing and the promised Holy Spirit. Their recipients and expressed sequence remain distinct.

Both name the Spirit as a pledge. Ephesians relates the pledge to inheritance and redemption of the possession; Corinthians relates it to God's preparing the speakers in the bodily-life argument. The accompanying images and objects are preserved.

Both report hearing of the readers' faith in Jesus and love toward all the saints. Ephesians names the Lord Jesus while Colossians names Christ Jesus; the correspondence does not identify their readerships as one congregation.

Both join thanksgiving for the readers with continuing prayer. Ephesians uses the writer's first-person singular remembrance; Colossians describes we giving thanks and praying. The letter situations and pronouns remain distinct.

Both prayers seek divinely given understanding. Ephesians asks the God of the Lord Jesus Christ, Father of glory, for a spirit of wisdom and revelation in knowing Him; Colossians asks for knowledge of His will in spiritual wisdom and understanding.

Both connect divine inheritance and hoped-for glory. Ephesians asks that the heart know the calling's hope and His inheritance's glory among the saints; Romans calls God's children heirs with Christ and anticipates revealed glory. The possessive wording and Romans’s suffering qualification remain distinct.

The later doxology again names power working in us. Here the prayer concerns the surpassing greatness of God's power toward believers; later God's ability exceeds asking or thinking. This is a recurring internal power theme rather than a second miracle report.

Both describe Christ raised from the dead and at God's right hand. Ephesians explicitly describes God exercising power and seating Him in heavenly places; Romans also names His death and intercession for us. Their additional claims remain distinct.

Both describe Christ's exaltation above every name. Philippians develops universal bending of knees and confession to God the Father's glory; Ephesians lists rule, authority, power and dominion across this age and the coming one. The lists and formulations differ.

The all-things-under-His-feet clause corresponds to the Psalm's subjection formula. Ephesians applies it to Christ and adds His headship for the Church; that Church clause is not supplied as part of the Psalm's creation-language setting.

Both explicitly call the Church Christ's body. Colossians names Him as its head and firstborn from the dead; Ephesians describes its fullness relation to the One who fills all things. The additional fullness wording is not silently inserted into the selected Colossians unit.

Both describe the recipients as dead in transgressions. Colossians also names uncircumcision and being made alive with forgiveness; the Ephesians sentence develops its own former-life description before reaching made-alive language in2:5.

Both describe hostile power associated with the age and disobedience or unbelief. Ephesians names the ruler of the air's authority and a working spirit; Corinthians names the god of this age blinding minds. The titles and actions are not treated as one verbatim formula.

Both look back on a former life directed by desires. Titus also lists deception, malice, envy and hatred; Ephesians speaks of flesh and thought and children of wrath by nature. The lists and the nature statement are not made identical.

Both locate salvation in divine mercy and love rather than the recipients' prior worthiness. Titus names God's kindness and love for humanity and saving mercy; Ephesians names God's abundant mercy and great love before its made-alive statement.

Both speak of people dead in transgressions being made alive together with Christ. Ephesians explicitly adds by grace you have been saved; Colossians also describes forgiving all transgressions. The additional clauses stay in their own passages.

Both refer to being raised together with Christ. Ephesians also says seated together in heavenly places in Christ; Colossians commands seeking what is above where Christ is seated at God's right hand. It does not explicitly say the readers are seated there in that unit.

The riches-of-His-grace wording recurs. Earlier it describes redemption through Christ's blood and forgiveness; here the future ages display surpassing grace's riches in kindness in Christ. The present benefit and future display remain distinct.

Both attribute salvation or justification to divine grace. Romans names being justified freely by His grace through redemption in Christ; Ephesians says saved by grace through faith and adds that this is not from yourselves but God's gift. The terms justification and salvation remain distinct.

Both exclude boasting in an argument about works and faith. Ephesians says not from works so no one boasts; Romans asks where boasting is and contrasts a law of works with a law of faith. The different law wording is preserved.

Both describe a divinely formed or redeemed people directed toward good works. Titus names Christ's self-giving to purify a people zealous for them; Ephesians names God's workmanship and prior preparation of the works to walk in. The actions differ.

Both discuss circumcision and flesh or hands. Ephesians recalls Gentile labels and circumcision made by hands in flesh; Colossians describes circumcision not made by hands in Christ. The physical description and Christ-centered metaphor remain distinct.

Israel, covenants and promise are explicitly connected in both. Romans lists Israelite privileges; Ephesians recalls Gentile alienation from Israel's commonwealth and promise covenants before the following nearness statement.

Both relate access or nearness to Jesus' blood. Ephesians describes formerly distant recipients made near by Christ's blood; Hebrews describes confidence to enter the holy places by Jesus' blood. The spatial images and addressed circumstances remain distinct.

Christ as our peace and the breaking of hostility correspond to making peace through the cross's blood in the reconciliation account. Ephesians focuses on both groups becoming one; Colossians names things on earth and in heaven. The scopes differ.

Both describe the removal of a barrier expressed through decrees. Ephesians names abolishing the law of commandments in decrees to create one new human being; Colossians names a hostile handwritten record removed at the cross. The law and record descriptions are not simply equated.

Both join reconciliation with Christ's bodily death. Ephesians says both are reconciled in one body to God through the cross; Colossians says in His fleshly body through death, with holy presentation as its aim. The body formulations are kept distinct.

The peace-to-far-and-near wording corresponds to Isaiah's peace saying. Ephesians presents Christ proclaiming it to the readers and those near; Isaiah's actual saying has its own Lord/healing context. The source is a scriptural echo rather than a supplied identical narrative event.

Both describe access through Jesus Christ. Ephesians explicitly says both have access in one Spirit to the Father; Romans joins access by faith into grace with peace toward God through the Lord Jesus Christ. The Spirit and faith formulations are not substituted for each other.

Both describe a community as a household. Ephesians contrasts foreigner status with being fellow citizens and God's household; Galatians gives the household of faith particular attention in doing good. The images and immediate purposes remain distinct.

The cornerstone image corresponds to Isaiah's chosen, precious cornerstone laid in Zion's foundations. Ephesians names Christ Jesus as cornerstone within its apostles-and-prophets foundation image; Isaiah's actual trust-in-it wording and setting are preserved rather than silently rewritten as the whole Ephesians sentence.

Both picture believers being built into a holy community. Ephesians describes the fitted building growing into a holy sanctuary; Peter's letter describes living stones and a spiritual house with priesthood and sacrifices. The added priestly details are not inserted into Ephesians.

Both describe the community as God's dwelling through the Spirit. Corinthians calls the readers God's temple with the Spirit dwelling among them; Ephesians describes their being built together into God's dwelling in the Spirit. The construction emphasis is specific here.
